title: Values, types, and coercion
runtime: Modern evergreen browser or Node.js with ES modules. Run fragments in browser DevTools or a small .js file unless the example says otherwise.

objectives.text: Separate a value from the variable that stores it.
Recognize the common primitive types and objects.
Predict explicit and implicit type conversion.

learningFlow: Explain the result in your own words

Review after two and seven days

sections.title: Values and variables
sections.body: A value is a piece of data, such as 42, "React", true, null, or an object. A variable is a named binding that can point to a value. typeof reports a broad runtime type, but typeof null is the historical string "object", so check null directly. JavaScript has primitive values and objects; primitives behave like indivisible values, while objects can hold changing properties.

sections.title: The types you will use
sections.body: The common primitive types are string, number, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, and symbol. Arrays, functions, dates, and plain records are objects; Array.isArray is the reliable array check. NaN is a number value that means a numeric calculation failed. Knowing the current type tells you which operations are meaningful.

sections.title: Conversion and coercion
sections.body: Explicit conversion names the intent: Number("12"), String(12), and Boolean(value). Implicit coercion happens when an operator needs another type. The + operator concatenates if a string is involved, so "5" + 2 becomes "52", while subtraction converts numeric strings and "5" - 2 becomes 3. Prefer explicit conversion at input boundaries so later code receives the type it expects.

sections.title: Truthy, falsy, and missing values
sections.body: Conditions convert values to boolean. false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, and NaN are falsy; most other values, including [] and {}, are truthy. A truthy check is useful for presence only when 0 or an empty string cannot be valid. Use exact checks when the difference between missing, empty, and zero matters.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: Values, types, and coercion is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain values, types, and coercion to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Separate a value from the variable that stores it. Recognize the common primitive types and objects. Predict explicit and implicit type conversion. Use truthy and falsy checks without losing valid data.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using values, types, and coercion behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can values, types, and coercion affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using values, types, and coercion produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
